section_title: Where can David turn when even his escape brings danger?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 Then David asked Ahimelech, “Is there not a spear or sword on hand here? For I have brought neither my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king’s mission was urgent.” 9 The priest replied, “The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the Valley of Elah, is here; it is wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you want, you may take it. For there is no other but this one here.” And David said, “There is none like it; give it to me.”

10 That day David fled from Saul and went to Achish king of Gath. 11 But the servants of Achish said to him, “Is this not David, the king of the land? Did they not sing about him in their dances, saying: ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands’?” 12 Now David took these words to heart and was very much afraid of Achish the king of Gath. 13 So he changed his behavior before them and feigned madness in their hands; he scratched on the doors of the gate and let his saliva run down his beard. 14 Then Achish said to his servants, “Look, you can see that the man is insane! Why have you brought him to me? 15 Am I in need of madmen, that you have brought this man to rave in my presence? Must this man come into my house?”

context_lines: David asks Ahimelech for a spear or sword, again saying that the king’s mission was urgent. The only available weapon is Goliath’s sword, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. David asks to take it. The weapon recalls the victory that first brought him into national attention.

He then goes to Achish, king of Gath. But Achish’s servants recognize him and repeat the song celebrating his victories. They even call him king of the land. The man escaping Israel’s king is now known among Israel’s enemies, and he becomes deeply afraid.

David pretends to be insane, scratching on the gate doors and letting saliva run down his beard. Achish reacts with irritation and refuses to welcome him into his house. The appearance of helplessness makes David seem unsuitable for the king’s company.

The scene is a sharp change from David facing Goliath. He is still the man God has chosen, but he is now a frightened fugitive whose reputation makes finding safety difficult. The passage shows his actions and fear without giving a full explanation of everything he hoped to achieve by entering Gath.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/21.htm) see Goliath’s sword as a reminder of God’s earlier deliverance as well as a useful weapon. On that reading, taking the sword need not mean David has abandoned trust in God. The object recalls what God has already done.

[Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/21.htm) views the behavior at Gath as a humiliating sign that David’s faith and courage are wavering. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/21.htm) instead allows the disguise as a strategy for escaping an enemy. The difference concerns how to assess his method of escape, rather than whether he pretended: the BSB explicitly says that he feigned madness.

[Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) allows that Achish may have recognized the performance and chosen to dismiss him anyway. [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/21.htm) treats the king as driving away someone he regards as unfit for his household. The text records Achish’s response without telling us whether he saw through the disguise.

The title king of the land is also read in more than one way. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/21.htm) discuss David’s prominence as Israel’s victorious commander as well as possible knowledge of his future kingship. The servants’ words show that he is famous; they do not tell us how much the speakers know about Samuel’s anointing.
god_plan_lines: The headings of [Psalm 56](https://biblehub.com/bsb/psalms/56.htm) and [Psalm 34](https://biblehub.com/bsb/psalms/34.htm) connect David’s prayers with danger in Gath and his feigned insanity. Psalm 34 names the ruler Abimelech, while this account calls him Achish. These psalms give us more than the outward scene: David brings fear to God, thanks Him for deliverance and teaches others to seek refuge in Him.

In [1 Peter 3:8–18](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_peter/3.htm), Peter takes up Psalm 34’s call to truthful speech, doing good and pursuing peace. He applies it to people facing hostility and directs them to honor Christ as Lord. Their hope rests in the righteous Christ, who suffered for the unrighteous to bring them to God.

This connection allows rescue and growth to stand together. David can thank God for bringing him through danger while learning how to live faithfully. The Christian hope Peter describes likewise includes God hearing His people, a clear conscience under pressure and salvation through Jesus; it does not depend on never feeling afraid.
